public.prompt: An operations manager prefers detail-oriented presentations. Which approach best fits this audience?

options.text: Start with the specifics of the analysis, then present next steps
Start with the high-level recommendation only
Alternate between high-level and detailed sections
Use only charts and visuals without text explanation

opt_detail_first.message: Correct. Technical or detail-oriented people like operations managers prefer to understand the specifics of an analysis first before considering next steps.

opt_high_level.message: Not quite. Operations managers are detail-oriented and typically want to understand the specifics of the analysis, not just a high-level recommendation.

opt_mixed.message: Not quite. For detail-oriented audiences, it's better to present the analysis systematically, starting with specifics, rather than alternating between levels.

opt_visual_only.message: Not quite. While visuals are helpful, detail-oriented audiences also want text explanations of the methodology and findings.

correct.message: Right. Tailoring to the audience means adjusting both the depth of detail and the order in which you present it.

incorrect.message: Remember: executives want the high-level arc first; detail-oriented audiences want to understand the specifics before considering recommendations.

hints: Think about whether each audience type prefers detail-first or recommendation-first.
Technical audiences typically want to understand the analysis before hearing recommendations.

public.prompt: Two versions of the Lagos finding are shown. Classify each version by its intended audience and identify the signal that reveals the target audience.

items.text: Version A: 'We recommend adding a second Lagos hub. Analysis shows 40% of deliveries exceed target time, with the longest delays in the eastern districts. A second hub would cut average delivery time by 18 minutes.'

Version B: 'Lagos delivery data shows 40% of orders exceed the 60-minute target. Eastern districts average 78 minutes (18 minutes over target). Peak delay hours are 2–5 PM. A second hub in the eastern zone would reduce average delivery time to 42 minutes, bringing 85% of deliveries within target.'

correct.message: Exactly right. Version A starts with the recommendation and provides high-level context — suited for an executive. Version B leads with detailed analysis and specifics — suited for an operations manager.

incorrect.message: Look at the order and density of information. Which version starts with the recommendation? Which version includes day-by-day breakdowns and specific numbers?

hints: Version A starts with 'We recommend' — what does that signal about the intended audience?
Version B includes specific time breakdowns and percentages — what type of audience prefers that level of detail?

public.prompt: Which addition to the Lagos report best addresses a likely question from the operations manager?

options.text: A detailed cost breakdown showing the investment required for a second hub
A comparison of QuickShip's delivery times to competitor benchmarks
A timeline showing how the second hub would be implemented
A note explaining how the delivery-time data was collected and validated

opt_cost_breakdown.message: Not the best fit. While cost matters, an operations manager is more likely to ask about the data quality and methodology behind the analysis before considering implementation costs.

opt_competitor.message: Not the best fit. Competitor benchmarks might be useful context, but an operations manager is more likely to first ask about the reliability of the data driving the recommendation.

opt_implementation.message: Not the best fit. Implementation details matter, but a detail-oriented operations manager will first want to understand how the data was collected and whether it is trustworthy.

opt_data_quality.message: Correct. Being tailored to the audience means anticipating their questions. A detail-oriented operations manager will likely ask about data quality and methodology before accepting the recommendation.

correct.message: Right. Detail-oriented audiences want to understand the specifics of how the analysis was done, including data quality and methodology.

incorrect.message: Think about what a detail-oriented operations manager would want to know first. They typically scrutinize the data and methodology before considering recommendations.

hints: What would a detail-oriented audience want to verify before trusting the recommendation?
Operations managers often ask about data quality and how the analysis was conducted.

public.prompt: For a detail-oriented audience, what is the benefit of presenting findings before making a request?

options.text: It prepares the audience to take in ideas about next steps and avoids derailing questions
It saves time by getting straight to the recommendation
It avoids questions by providing all the details upfront
It simplifies the message by reducing the amount of information

opt_builds_trust.message: Correct. Technical or detail-oriented people prefer to understand the specifics of an analysis first, so they are prepared to take in ideas about next steps. This can also avoid the audience derailing the presentation with questions.

opt_saves_time.message: Not quite. For detail-oriented audiences, presenting findings first actually takes more time initially, but it builds the foundation they need to accept the recommendation.

opt_avoids_questions.message: Not quite. While presenting findings first can help avoid derailing questions, the primary benefit is that it prepares detail-oriented audiences to take in ideas about next steps.

opt_simplifies.message: Not quite. Presenting findings first actually adds more information, not less. The benefit is that it prepares detail-oriented audiences to accept the recommendation.

correct.message: Exactly. Detail-oriented audiences want to understand the specifics first so they are prepared to consider next steps. This sequence builds trust.

incorrect.message: Remember: detail-oriented audiences prefer to understand the analysis before hearing recommendations. This prepares them to accept the request.

hints: Think about what detail-oriented audiences need before they can accept a recommendation.
Presenting findings first helps the audience feel prepared and builds credibility.

public.intro: The table shows average delivery times and order volumes for three cities across two months. Use it to identify which rows represent data that anticipates stakeholder questions about the Lagos finding.

tasks.prompt: Select the row that would help answer a stakeholder's question about data quality or measurement methodology.
Select the row that would help address a stakeholder's question about alternative explanations for the pattern.
Select the row that would help address a stakeholder's question about implementation risks or unintended consequences.

task_data_quality.correct: Correct. The Lagos Month 1 baseline shows the starting point, which helps establish the data quality and measurement consistency.
task_data_quality.incorrect: Not quite. Look for a row that establishes a baseline or comparison point for data quality.

task_alternative_explanation.correct: Correct. The Abuja data shows a different city with similar delivery patterns, which helps rule out Lagos-specific factors as the sole explanation.
task_alternative_explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Look for a row that shows a comparison to help rule out alternative explanations.

task_implementation_risk.correct: Correct. The Lagos Month 2 data shows the current problem state, which helps illustrate the urgency and risk of inaction.
task_implementation_risk.incorrect: Not quite. Look for a row that shows the current state or potential consequence.

correct.message: Excellent. You identified the rows that anticipate stakeholder questions: data quality (baseline), alternative explanations (comparison), and implementation risks (current state).

incorrect.message: Look for rows that address questions a stakeholder might ask: How was this measured? What else could explain this? What are the risks?

hints: Stakeholders often ask about data quality and baseline measurements.
Detail-oriented audiences want to know about alternative explanations and potential risks.

public.prompt: Three slides from the Lagos presentation are shown out of order. Which order places them correctly into opening–body–call to action?

options.text: Slide A (context/situation) → Slide B (finding + evidence) → Slide C (call to action)
Slide B (finding + evidence) → Slide A (context/situation) → Slide C (call to action)
Slide C (call to action) → Slide A (context/situation) → Slide B (finding + evidence)
Slide A (context/situation) → Slide C (call to action) → Slide B (finding + evidence)

opt_context_finding_action.message: Correct. A presentation should have an obvious beginning (context/situation), middle (finding + evidence), and end (call to action).

opt_finding_context_action.message: Not quite. The beginning should establish the context of the situation before presenting findings. Starting with findings leaves the audience without necessary background.

opt_action_context_finding.message: Not quite. The call to action should come at the end, after the context and findings have been established. Starting with the request leaves the audience unprepared.

opt_context_action_finding.message: Not quite. The call to action should come at the end, after the findings have been presented. Placing it before the findings means the audience has not yet seen the evidence supporting the request.

correct.message: Right. The structure is opening (context), body (finding + evidence), and call to action (what is being asked).

incorrect.message: Remember the three-part structure: beginning (context), middle (finding + evidence), end (call to action).

hints: The beginning should establish the context before presenting findings.
The call to action comes at the end, after the evidence has been presented.

public.prompt: Drag the five Lagos presentation elements into the correct opening–body–call-to-action order.

items.text: QuickShip's Lagos operations have grown 40% in the past year
40% of deliveries now exceed the 60-minute target
Eastern districts average 78 minutes, 18 minutes over target
A second hub in the eastern zone would reduce average delivery time to 42 minutes
We recommend approving the second hub by end of quarter

correct.message: Perfect. You organized the elements into the correct structure: opening (context + problem), body (evidence + solution), and call to action (request).

incorrect.message: Think about the three-part structure. The opening establishes context, the body presents findings and evidence, and the end states what is being asked.

hints: Start with context to establish the situation.
Present the problem and evidence in the middle.
End with the solution and what you are asking for.

public.prompt: Four executive summary drafts are shown. Which one best follows the taught structure?

options.text: Draft A: Has a takeaway title, uses section headers ('Finding' and 'Recommendation'), and presents content in prose paragraphs
Draft B: Has a descriptive title, uses bullet points throughout, and covers findings and recommendations
Draft C: Has a takeaway title and prose paragraphs, but no section headers to distinguish findings from recommendations
Draft D: Has section headers and prose, but runs to four pages with extensive detail

opt_structured.message: Correct. An executive summary should have a takeaway title, section headers to group content into easily-discernible sections, and prose paragraphs rather than bullets.

opt_bullets.message: Not quite. While bullet points are common, the taught structure uses prose paragraphs with section headers. Bullets can make the summary feel like a list rather than a narrative.

opt_no_headers.message: Not quite. Section headers are important for grouping content into easily-discernible sections. Without them, the reader has to work harder to distinguish findings from recommendations.

opt_long.message: Not quite. An executive summary should be a one- or two-page overview, not four pages. The goal is to provide a concise summary, not extensive detail.

correct.message: Right. The executive summary structure includes a takeaway title, section headers, and prose paragraphs — all within one or two pages.

incorrect.message: Remember the key elements: a takeaway title, section headers to group content, prose paragraphs, and a one- or two-page length.

hints: Section headers help the reader quickly identify findings and recommendations.
Prose paragraphs create a narrative arc rather than a list.
An executive summary should be concise — one or two pages.

public.instruction:
Using the Lagos scenario below, write a brief executive summary with a title, a Finding section (one sentence), and a Recommendation section (one sentence). Your summary should:
• Have a title that states the main takeaway
• Include a 'Finding' section header followed by one sentence describing the delivery-time problem
• Include a 'Recommendation' section header followed by one sentence proposing the second hub
• Use prose (not bullets)
• Be concise (approximately 50–75 words total)

rubric.criterion: Title states main takeaway (e.g., 'Second Lagos Hub Needed to Meet Delivery Targets')
Includes a 'Finding' section header followed by a sentence describing the delivery-time problem
Includes a 'Recommendation' section header followed by a sentence proposing the second hub
Uses prose paragraphs rather than bullet points
The summary is concise (approximately 50–75 words) and focused on the key points

correct.message: Excellent work. Your executive summary follows the taught structure with a takeaway title, section headers, and prose paragraphs.

incorrect.message: Review the structure: a takeaway title, 'Finding' and 'Recommendation' section headers, and prose paragraphs (not bullets).

hints: Start with a title that states the main takeaway, not just a description.
Use section headers ('Finding' and 'Recommendation') to organize your content.
Write in prose paragraphs, not bullet points.
Keep it concise — aim for 50–75 words total.
